GEOLOGICAL SETTING The Late Precambrian and Early Paleozoic geological sequence preserved in Cape Breton Island, summarized in Figures 1 and 2, comprises Late Hadrynian basement volcanics and granites overlain by well- preserved Cambrian to Lower Ordovician shallow-water marine clastics and volcanics. The lithologic and faunal characteristics of these rocks and their correlation with similar strata found along strike in the northern Appalachians, particularly in eastern Newfoundland (see Figure la), have been discussed by many authors [e.g., Henningsmoen, 1969; Rast et al., 1976; Williams, 1978]. The assemblage of often geographically separate localities where similar rocks occur has been called the Avalon terrane by Williams and Hatcher [1983], named after the Avalon peninsula of Newfoundland. The Cambrian volcanics present in the Boisdale Peninsula (Bourinot Group) were the principal focus of our study. These volcanics comprise flows and volcanogenic sedimentary rocks, which appear to have had a restricted areal extent at the time they were formed [Keppie and Dostal, 1980; Hutchinson, 1952]. They have been related 632 Johnson and Van der Voo: Cambrian Paleomagnetism, Avalon by Hutchinson [1952] to a volcanic

SAMPL I NG The Bourinot volcanics and sediments are exposed in stream sections in the southern Boisdale peninsula, and in railroad cuts, along the shore of St. Andrews Channel, and on Long Island (see Figure 1, sites 13,31-33) in the north part of the peninsula. Initial reconnaissance sampling in the Bourinot Group was concentrated in sediments of varying lithology exposed in the stream sections along Gregwa, Dugald, Macmullin, and Gillis Brooks. Different lithologies represented here probably reflect varying source materials since fossils preserved in different beds are similar [Hutchinson, 1952]. These streams were later resampled in detail (see Figure 1) with each site restricted to a single bed or a few beds with similar lithology. Volcanic flows immediately underlying or interbedded with sediments were sampled at Dugald and Gillis Brooks (see Figures lc and ld), as well as in the north part of the study area. A similar agglomerate unit was sampled at Gregwa Brook (site B01) and at MacMullin Brook (B25) and may represent the same unit [Hutchinson, 1952]; however, other stratigraphic units, whether volcanic or sedimentary, were not uniquely correlated between localities. PALEOMAGNETIC RESULTS Paleomagnetic specimens, prepared from oriented core and block samples, were demagnetized using standard alternating field (AF) and thermal methods. The results were analyzed using orthogonal projection diagrams [Zijderveld, 1967]. Initial AF and thermal demagnetization results for specimens from the same rock unit showed that magnetization components resolved by thermal treatment were not separated using AF. The majority of the remaining specimens were therefore thermally demagnetized. Demagnetization data for specimens not yielding stable endpoints in thermal treatment were further examined for coplanarity of successive vector endpoints, using the remagnetization-circle method of Halls [1976,1978] and Bailey and Halls [1984]. Site B32 on Long Island was taken in a basalt dike cutting some rhyolites, which was inferred to be a feeder dike for a basalt higher in the section. Almost all of the flows in the southern part of the peninsula show visible oxidation, including flows at B16,16', which were deposited subareally, and B28,30, which were deposited in shallow water. The conditions during deposition of the flow at B17 are less certain because it is underlain and overlain by marine sediments; however, the conspicuous hematite staining in the underlying siltstone, which contrasts with other sediments in the section [Hutchinson, 1952], suggests subareal exposure of the surface on which the overlying flow was deposited. Only the youngest flow occurring at Dugald Brook (site B18; see Figure lc) was not visibly oxidized, and this may be the result of a faster rate of deposition and burial. Volcanics in the northern part of the peninsula exhibit varying degrees of oxidation, but in general, younger flows in the sequence show better preservation; the flows and dike sampled near the top of the sequence here were relatively fresh. The use of dual-polarity magnetizations in the fold test is justified because the opposite polarity magnetizations indicated in Figure 6 were observed in separate flows on different limbs of the fold. Both polarities were observed in separate hematite-bearing (oxidized) flows, as well as in separate magnetite-bearing (unoxidized) flows. The similar directions in oxidized and unoxidized flows imply a similar age for their magnetizations. These include early investigations of Late Precambrian strata in Newfoundland [Nairn et al., 1959] and New Brunswick [Black, 1964] . GEOLOGICAL SETTING The Late Precambrian and Early Paleozoic geological sequence preserved in Cape Breton Island, summarized in Figures 1 and 2, comprises Late Hadrynian basement volcanics and granites overlain by well- preserved Cambrian to Lower Ordovician shallow-water marine clastics and volcanics. The lithologic and faunal characteristics of these rocks and their correlation with similar strata found along strike in the northern Appalachians, particularly in eastern Newfoundland (see Figure la), have been discussed by many authors [e.g., Henningsmoen, 1969; Rast et al., 1976; Williams, 1978]. The assemblage of often geographically separate localities where similar rocks occur has been called the Avalon terrane by Williams and Hatcher [1983], named after the Avalon peninsula of Newfoundland. The Cambrian volcanics present in the Boisdale Peninsula (Bourinot Group) were the principal focus of our study. These volcanics comprise flows and volcanogenic sedimentary rocks, which appear to have had a restricted areal extent at the time they were formed [Keppie and Dostal, 1980; Hutchinson, 1952]. Interbedded volcanics and sediments of the Bourinot Group (Mid- Cambrian) in central Cape Breton Island were studied as part of a paleomagnetic investigation to quantify the geologically plausible displacements of the Avalon terrane with respect to the North American craton. Both volcanics and sediments reveal prefolding magnetizations with steep to intermediate inclinations. Dual- polarity magnetizations in different volcanic flows are probably primary and they yield a mean direction of D=293 ø, I=-66 ø (N=9, k=41.8, 95=8.1 ø) . The sediments reveal, upon detailed thermal demagnetization, complex multivectorial remanences. Initial reduction of the data involves processing with principal component analysis (PCA) [Kirschvink, 1980] using a 10 ø maximum angular deviation (MAD) cutoff. From the orthogonal plots and the PCA the multicomponent nature of the magnetizations present in these volcanics was apparent. Both magnetite and haematite are major remanence carriers. The selection criteria applied to the PCA directions was designed to eliminate spurious components as far as possible due to viscous remanent magnetization (VRM) or isothermal remanent magnetization (IRM). High natural remanent magnetization (NRM) intensities indicate that lightning has played a large role in magnetizing some of the samples collected. Therefore, only components stable above at least 500øC have been considered, and, when AF demagnetization was used, only the components of highest coercivity have been considered. To ensure objectivity and to increase the quality of the result, the data have been passed through a final filter, namely, only sites for which at least three samples have yielded similar directions after applying the above selection criteria have been used for the statistical computations. These outcrops include intrusive rocks in the Ortiz Mountains and Cerrillos Hills and extrusive flows in the Hagan embayment, in the Cienega area, and in Arroyo Hondo south of Santa Fe. The intrusive rocks are found within a sequence of prerift Mesozoic and early Cenozoic sedimentary rocks. Early Paleozoic paleomagnetic data from the Carolina slate belt should indicate whether this island arc was part of Laurentia or Avalon, or was an independent terrane during this time. Throughout the Carolina slate belt, the primary Precambrian to Cambrian magnetizations have been destroyed by metamorphism. This study and that of Noel et al. [1987] are first efforts at correlating high blocking temperature magnetization 40 .39 - components to Ar/ Ar plateau ages in Carolina slate belt rocks. The exposed sedimentary rocks of southern Umnak Island (Figure 2b) consist of about 300 m of thin-bedded laminated siltstone, mudstone, and very fine grained sandstone of mainly volcaniclastic composition. Strata are gently folded and dips rarely exceed 10 ø . The thickest, most continuous exposures are along Driftwood Bay and Starr Point where palynomorphs and dinofiagellates suggest a late Eocene to early Oligocene age of deposition [McLean and Hein, 1984]. Siltstone and mudstone consist of varying proportions of tuff (glassy volcanic debris) and angular grains of calcic plagioclase, rare quartz, augitc, and opaque minerals. In most rocks the tuffaceous component is altered to smectite and more rarely to zeolite minerals, while calcic plagioclase and augitc remain unaltered. A low-temperature diagenesis of the sediments is suggested by preservation of calcic plagioclase, the presence of low-temperature zeolites (heulandite and analcime), and light-colored palynomorphs. This early paleomagnetic data from the Peninsular and Prince William terranes in southern Alaska (Figure 1) suggested that these terranes may not have accreted to the North American plate until the middle or late Tertiary [Stone and Packer, 1977, 1979; Stone et al., 1982a]. However, thermal alteration of sampled units, complex geological structure, and demagnetization of only a small number of samples made tectonic interpretation of many of the previous paleomagnetic studies difficult [Coe et al., 1985]. In addition, the geometry of the large Zodiac sediment fan in the northeast Pacific basin suggests poleward transport of the Aleutian arc [Scholl et al., 1977; Byrne, 1979; Stevenson et al., 1983; Moore et al., 1983]. The exposed sedimentary rocks of southern Umnak Island (Figure 2b) consist of about 300 m of thin-bedded laminated siltstone, mudstone, and very fine grained sandstone of mainly volcaniclastic composition. Strata are gently folded and dips rarely exceed 10 ø . The thickest, most continuous exposures are along Driftwood Bay and Starr Point where palynomorphs and dinofiagellates suggest a late Eocene to early Oligocene age of deposition [McLean and Hein, 1984]. This early paleomagnetic data from the Peninsular and Prince William terranes in southern Alaska (Figure 1) suggested that these terranes may not have accreted to the North American plate until the middle or late Tertiary [Stone and Packer, 1977, 1979; Stone et al., 1982a]. However, thermal alteration of sampled units, complex geological structure, and demagnetization of only a small number of samples made tectonic interpretation of many of the previous paleomagnetic studies difficult [Coe et al., 1985]. In addition, the geometry of the large Zodiac sediment fan in the northeast Pacific basin suggests poleward transport of the Aleutian arc [Scholl et al., 1977; Byrne, 1979; Stevenson et al., 1983; Moore et al., 1983]. In addition, tholeiitic basalts [Blackadar, 1964; Fricker, 1963; Williamson and Van Wagoner, 1985] appear either as lava flows or as sills and dykes. Early phases of effusive activity are recorded by the Upper Carboniferous Audhild and Lower Permian Esayoo basalts on the northwestern edge of the Basin on Axel Heiberg and Ellesmere islands. The main, Cretaceous phases [Osadetz and Ricketts, 1985] occurred between 130 to 90 Ma in the (1) Valangian to AptJan (Isachsen Formation), affecting the largest area, from Ellef Ringnes Island in the west to northwestern Ellesmere Island in the east; (2) late Albian to early Cennomanian (Hassel Formation), recorded by lava flows on Amund Ringnes Island [Balkwill

xis, although the general trend is northeast-southwest to east-west. A syncline, cut by three dykes, also occurs along the hanging wall side of the Van Hauen Thrust Fault (Figure 4). Bjarnasson Island contains a thinner, generally coarser-grained basin marginal section; unfortunately, only three sills in Middle Triassic shale could be sampled due to severe weather conditions. The sills preferentially appear in Middle-Upper Triassic black shale, often forming prominent ridges that can be followed for tens of kilometers, and are completely absent in Jurassic and Cretaceous sediments in this part of the Sverdrup Basin. Field and air photo observations indicate that a particular sill generally can be followed along strike for no more than a few kilometers, after which it tapers out and another, slightly overlapping sill may appear immediately below or above. Thus the sills do not appear as large sheets, covering many square kilometers, but rather as \"leaves\" branching out from what must be an extensive, interconnected magma supply system. Locally, sills may climb by cutting the strata at a low angle or, as seen in excellent cliff exposures along Buchanan Lake immediately north of section II, by abruptly turning into a dyke 19449194, 1988, 3, Downloaded

In this paper we do not attempt to formulate a new tectonic model; rather, the objective of our study is to provide a new and independent paleomagnetic data set by which various aspects of proposed models may be tested. SAMPLING LOCALITIES We have collected samples from three widely separated localities in Haiti. These are designated from north to south as Ennery, Beloc, and Les Cayes [Figure 1]. A \"locality\" consists of several sites, each of which in turn represents 7-11 cored samples. Sites within a locality are distributed about an area of a few square kilometers; a distri- bution that will become important in our final synthesis and interpretation of the paleomagnetic data. Samples were obtained in the field using a portable rock coring drill. At the Beloc locality we used the oriented-block method to collect the less consolidated chalk lithologies. All orientations were made using the Brunton compass, and at each site we were careful to sample only the freshest appearing materials. Field information regarding the number of sites and number of samples at each locality is included in Table 1. Ennery Eoce

An almost complete sequence of strata with ages from early Paleogene to Quaternary is well preserved in the Oga Peninsula, on the western side of northeast Honshu at about t0 ø north latitude (Figure 1), making the Oga Peninsula a type locality for the Ter- tiary sequence in Northeast Japan. Tertiary formations, arranged in monoclinal beds of strata, are well exposed along the west coast of the penin- sula (Figure lb). Geological units ofthe Oga Peninsula are roughly divided into two groups [Takayasu and Matoba, 1976]. Older formations (basement, Akashima, Monzen, and Daijhna Formations) mainly consist of vokanic rocks and become younger to the south. Younger formations (Nishikurosawa, Onnagawa, Funakawa, and Kitaura For- mations) are composed of sedimentary rocks and become younger to the east. cal units ofthe Oga Peninsula are roughly divided into two groups [Takayasu and Matoba, 1976]. Older formations (basement, Akashima, Monzen, and Daijhna Formations) mainly consist of vokanic rocks and become younger to the south. Younger formations (Nishikurosawa, Onnagawa, Funakawa, and Kitaura For- mations) are composed of sedimentary rocks and become younger to the east. The most recent vokanic rocks are Kanpuzan lava flows erupted in the Quaternary. As shown in Figure 2, over 30 age determinations made by different methods (K-At and fission track methods) give consistent results [Kaneoka, 1983a]. We adopted as the age of each formation the mean value of the reported ages as suggested by Kaneoka [1983a]. The ages of the younger sedimentary formations were estimated from biostratigraphic studies as sumrealized by Tsuchl [1981]. Previous paleomagnetic studies in the Oga Peninsula were mainly concerned with the magnetostratigraphy of the younger sedimentary rocks [Kent, 1973; Kimura, 1974; Kitazato, 1975]. In this area, a total of 26 sites were sampled, and six or more core samples were obtained at each site by using a gasoline-powered drilling apparatus. An almost complete sequence of strata with ages from early Paleogene to Quaternary is well preserved in the Oga Peninsula, on the western side of northeast Honshu at about t0 ø north latitude (Figure 1), making the Oga Peninsula a type locality for the Ter- tiary sequence in Northeast Japan. Tertiary formations, arranged in monoclinal beds of strata, are well exposed along the west coast of the penin- sula (Figure lb). Geological units ofthe Oga Peninsula are roughly divided into two groups [Takayasu and Matoba, 1976]. Older formations (basement, Akashima, Monzen, and Daijhna Formations) mainly consist of vokanic rocks and become younger to the south. Younger formations (Nishikurosawa, Onnagawa, Funakawa, and Kitaura For- mations) are composed of sedimentary rocks and become younger to the east. cal units ofthe Oga Peninsula are roughly divided into two groups [Takayasu and Matoba, 1976]. Older formations (basement, Akashima, Monzen, and Daijhna Formations) mainly consist of vokanic rocks and become younger to the south. Younger formations (Nishikurosawa, Onnagawa, Funakawa, and Kitaura For- mations) are composed of sedimentary rocks and become younger to the east. The most recent vokanic rocks are Kanpuzan lava flows erupted in the Quaternary. As shown in Figure 2, over 30 age determinations made by different methods (K-At and fission track methods) give consistent results [Kaneoka, 1983a]. We adopted as the age of each formation the mean value of the reported ages as suggested by Kaneoka [1983a]. The ages of the younger sedimentary formations were estimated from biostratigraphic studies as sumrealized by Tsuchl [1981]. Previous paleomagnetic studies in the Oga Peninsula were mainly concerned with the magnetostratigraphy of the younger sedimentary rocks [Kent, 1973; Kimura, 1974; Kitazato, 1975]. In this area, a total of 26 sites were sampled, and six or more core samples were obtained at each site by using a gasoline-powered drilling apparatus. We have made a paleomagnetic study of Ter- tiary rocks from the Oga Peninsula, northers Honshu Is- land. Vokanic and sedimentary rocks were sampled from 26 sites in the peninsula. The ages of the rocks range from 62 Ma to the present. The resuRs indicate a couaterclock- wise rotation of Northeast Japan with respect to eastern Asia around a pole at 58øN, 149øE, between about 22 Ma and 15 Ms. The amount of the rotation is about 20 ø. For Northeast Japan, Tosha [1983] and Otofuji et aL [1985] recently made paleomagnetic studies. Geological units ofthe Oga Peninsula are roughly divided into two groups [Takayasu and Matoba, 1976]. Older formations (basement, Akashima, Monzen, and Daijhna Formations) mainly consist of vokanic rocks and become younger to the south. Younger formations (Nishikurosawa, Onnagawa, Funakawa, and Kitaura For- mations) are composed of sedimentary rocks and become younger to the east. cal units ofthe Oga Peninsula are roughly divided into two groups [Takayasu and Matoba, 1976]. Older formations (basement, Akashima, Monzen, and Daijhna Formations) mainly consist of vokanic rocks and become younger to the south. Younger formations (Nishikurosawa, Onnagawa, Funakawa, and Kitaura For- mations) are composed of sedimentary rocks and become younger to the east. The most recent vokanic rocks are Kanpuzan lava flows erupted in the Quaternary. As shown in Figure 2, over 30 age determinations made by different methods (K-At and fission track methods) give consistent results [Kaneoka, 1983a]. We adopted as the age of each formation the mean value of the reported ages as suggested by Kaneoka [1983a]. Previous paleomagnetic studies in the Oga Peninsula were mainly concerned with the magnetostratigraphy of the younger sedimentary rocks [Kent, 1973; Kimura, 1974; Kitazato, 1975]. On the other hand, other samples show nor- real directions. We adopt the normal direction as the pale- omagnetic field direction for the basement. The direction is close to that of the Akashima Formation and the present geomagnetic field. Hence the effect of the VRM compo- nent should also be examined. Thermomagnetic analysis for the rocks close to and fax from the contact indicates that they have a Curie temperature of about 600øC, in- dicating magnetite as the main magnetic phase in these rocks. It is also inferred that heating of the basement rocks due to the dike intrusion did not severely affect the magnetic minerals in the rocks. The VRM component in the reversely magnetized samples can be demagnetized by an AF field of 5 mT or a temperature of 200øC. Assuming that the coercivity and the blocking temperature spectra of the magnetite in these rocks were also unchanged by the heating, this suggests that the stable component of the basement is not a VRM. An almost complete sequence of strata with ages from early Paleogene to Quaternary is well preserved in the Oga Peninsula, on the western side of northeast Honshu at about t0 ø north latitude (Figure 1), making the Oga Peninsula a type locality for the Ter- tiary sequence in Northeast Japan. Tertiary formations, arranged in monoclinal beds of strata, are well exposed along the west coast of the penin- sula (Figure lb). Geological units ofthe Oga Peninsula are roughly divided into two groups [Takayasu and Matoba, 1976]. Older formations (basement, Akashima, Monzen, and Daijhna Formations) mainly consist of vokanic rocks and become younger to the south. Younger formations (Nishikurosawa, Onnagawa, Funakawa, and Kitaura For- mations) are composed of sedimentary rocks and become younger to the east. cal units ofthe Oga Peninsula are roughly divided into two groups [Takayasu and Matoba, 1976]. Older formations (basement, Akashima, Monzen, and Daijhna Formations) mainly consist of vokanic rocks and become younger to the south. Younger formations (Nishikurosawa, Onnagawa, Funakawa, and Kitaura For- mations) are composed of sedimentary rocks and become younger to the east. The most recent vokanic rocks are Kanpuzan lava flows erupted in the Quaternary. As shown in Figure 2, over 30 age determinations made by different methods (K-At and fission track methods) give consistent results [Kaneoka, 1983a]. We adopted as the age of each formation the mean value of the reported ages as suggested by Kaneoka [1983a]. The ages of the younger sedimentary formations were estimated from biostratigraphic studies as sumrealized by Tsuchl [1981]. Previous paleomagnetic studies in the Oga Peninsula were mainly concerned with the magnetostratigraphy of the younger sedimentary rocks [Kent, 1973; Kimura, 1974; Kitazato, 1975]. In this area, a total of 26 sites were sampled, and six or more core samples were obtained at each site by using a gasoline-powered drilling apparatus. Geological units ofthe Oga Peninsula are roughly divided into two groups [Takayasu and Matoba, 1976]. Older formations (basement, Akashima, Monzen, and Daijhna Formations) mainly consist of vokanic rocks and become younger to the south. Younger formations (Nishikurosawa, Onnagawa, Funakawa, and Kitaura For- mations) are composed of sedimentary rocks and become younger to the east. It is a thick sequence of mainly terrestrial deposits with a maximum thickness of about 2700 m, estimated from the Parkes Syncline [Conoily, 1965]. Three subgroups are further divided according to their lithological characters: in stratigraphic order these are the Beargamil Subgroup, the Nangar Subgroup, and the Cookamidgera Subgroup. Both the basal and the top subgroups are continental facies, dominated by red measures. The middle subgroup has marine intercalations at the bottom [Williams, 1977; C. Powell and D. Crane, unpublished work, 1980], and is characterized by repetitious cycles of white quartzose sandstones, red and white sandstones with some red siltstones, and then red siltstones and shales. The Hervey Group unconformably overlies the mid-Devonian granite and other older Palaeozoic rocks in this region, while fish plates from the middle part of the sequence, e.g., the Nangar Subgroup, indicate a Late Devonian age [Conoily, 1965]. Three subgroups are further divided according to their lithological characters: in stratigraphic order these are the Beargamil Subgroup, the Nangar Subgroup, and the Cookamidgera Subgroup. Both the basal and the top subgroups are continental facies, dominated by red measures. The middle subgroup has marine intercalations at the bottom [Williams, 1977; C. Powell and D. The Hervey Group unconformably overlies the mid-Devonian granite and other older Palaeozoic rocks in this region, while fish plates from the middle part of the sequence, e.g., the Nangar Subgroup, indicate a Late Devonian age [Conoily, 1965]. The Hervey Group, together with the underlying rocks, was deformed during the mid-Carboniferous Kanimblan Orogeny (C. Powell and E. Scheibner, personal communication, 1987). The folds generally trend north-south (Figure 1). High-angle reverse faults are found cutting through the formations. Cleavage is not visible in most of the area but is well developed in the pelttic units and some sandstones at the southern part of the Hervey Syncline and the Murga area southeast of Parkes. THE CAMBRIAN POSITION OF THE NORTH CHINA BLOCK The suggested southern hemisphere position for the NCB might seem to be strange, so that further explanation is necessary. In the NCB there is a great sedimentary hiatus from Upper Ordovician to Lower Carboniferous. The oldest post-Cambrian pole with known polarity is the Permian pole (McElhinny et al., 1981; Lin, 1984). If we assume that the apparent polar wander was less than 90 degrees from the Cambrian to the Permian, which seems reasonable in the light of the APW paths for the other continents, then the polarity ambiguity of the Cambrian pole can be resolved. If the Nicola Volcanics had been hematized before the mid-Cretaceous, then their B component would indicate a similar rotation and translation to that found for their A com- ponent and for the Guichon and Copper Mountain plutons. Correcting the B component for this rotation and translation moves its pole to an PALEOMAGNETISM OF THE TRIASSIC NICOLA VOLCANICS 241 untenable position in the Pacific Ocean off the apparent polar wander (APW) path for the North American craton (Irving, 1979). Therefore, the most likely age for the origin of the post-tilting B component is Middle Eocene, coincident with extrusion of the Princeton Group volcanics. Relative to the Eocene reference pole for the craton, this suggests that ~ 15 ° of the clockwise rotation and ~7 ° of the northward translation of Quesnellia occurred during Eocene and Oligocene time. Combined with previous paleomagnetic data, these results indicate that Quesnellia was translated northward by ~ 13 ° of paleoatitude along with the rest of Terrane I and rotated ~45 ° clockwise during Late Cretaceous to Oligocene time with ~7 ° of the translation and 15 ° of the rotation occurring during Eocene to Oligocene time. INTRODUCTION The Upper Triassic Nicola Volcanics are the oldest extrusive rocks exposed in the Quesnellia Subterrane of allochthonous composite Terrane I (Monger et al., 1982) in southcentral British Columbia (Fig. 1). Paleomagnetic studies on Lower Jurassic plutons have shown that Quesnellia has been translated northward by ,-~ 13 ° of paleolatitude and rotated clockwise by --~43 ° between Late Cretaceous and pre-Miocene time (Symons, 1973, 1983a) as part of the overall motion of Terrane I (Monger and Irving, 1980; Symons, 1983b) and of the Cordillera overall (e.g., Beck et al., 1981). Paleomagnetic data locations include the Takla Volcanics (TA), Hazelton Volcanics (HZ), Axelgold Intrusion (AX), Topley Intrusions (TO), Cariboo Lavas (CL), Cariboo Plugs (CP), Guichon Batholith (GB), Nicola Volcanics (NV) and Copper Mountain Intrusions (CM). GEOLOGY The Nicola Group is exposed in three north-trending belts bounded by major faults (Fig. 2). The Central Belt was deposited first and it is com- prised of subaerial and submarine andesites and basalts, breccias, con- glomerates and lahars with minor comagmatic diorite and syenite intrusions. The Eastern Belt consists of volcanic sedimentary rocks, lahars with minor basalt flows and syenite stocks. The Western Belt was deposited last and it is comprised of andesitic to rhyolitic flows and pyroclastics with interbeds of limestone, volcanic conglomerate and sandstone. Paleomagnetism of the Triassic Nicola Volcanics and geotectonics of the Quesnellia Subterrane of Terrane I, British Columbia. Journal of Geodynamics, 2: 229-244. The Triassic Nicola Volcanics are the oldest strata in the QuesneUia Subterrane of composite Terrane I which is located in the southcentral Cordillera of British Columbia. A paleomagnetic study using AF and thermal demagnetization methods of 563 speciments from 56 sites in three petrologically and tec- tonically distinct belts of the Nicola isolates two remanence components residing dominantly in hematite. The prefolding A component found after 560°C thermal cleaning gives a pole position of I1.3°W, 52.7°N (60=4.7 °, 6 m =7.2°), and appears to be caused by alteration associated with major Early Jurassic intrusive events. The dominant postfolding B component is best defined by 565°C thermal cleaning and gives a pole of 303.0°W, 82.5°N (60 = 6.6 °, 6m = 8.6°). It likely reflects alteration associated with Eocene volcanism. Combined with previous paleomagnetic data

ent is best defined by 565°C thermal cleaning and gives a pole of 303.0°W, 82.5°N (60 = 6.6 °, 6m = 8.6°). It likely reflects alteration associated with Eocene volcanism. Combined with previous paleomagnetic data, these results indicate that Quesnellia was translated northward by ~ 13 ° of paleoatitude along with the rest of Terrane I and rotated ~45 ° clockwise during Late Cretaceous to Oligocene time with ~7 ° of the translation and 15 ° of the rotation occurring during Eocene to Oligocene time. INTRODUCTION The Upper Triassic Nicola Volcanics are the oldest extrusive rocks exposed in the Quesnellia Subterrane of allochthonous composite Terrane I (Monger et al., 1982) in southcentral British Columbia (Fig. 1). Paleomagnetic studies on Lower Jurassic plutons have shown that Quesnellia has been translated northward by ,-~ 13 ° of paleolatitude and rotated clockwise by --~43 ° between Late Cretaceous and pre-Miocene time (Symons, 1973, 1983a) as part of the overall motion of Terrane I (Monger and Irving, 1980; Symons, 1983b) and of the Cordillera overall (e.g., Beck et al., 1981). Paleomagnetic data locations include the Takla Volcanics (TA), Hazelton Volcanics (HZ), Axelgold Intrusion (AX), Topley Intrusions (TO), Cariboo Lavas (CL), Cariboo Plugs (CP), Guichon Batholith (GB), Nicola Volcanics (NV) and Copper Mountain Intrusions (CM). GEOLOGY The Nicola Group is exposed in three north-trending belts bounded by major faults (Fig. 2). The Central Belt was deposited first and it is com- prised of subaerial and submarine andesites and basalts, breccias, con- glomerates and lahars with minor comagmatic diorite and syenite intrusions. The Eastern Belt consists of volcanic sedimentary rocks, lahars with minor basalt flows and syenite stocks. The Western Belt was deposited last and it is comprised of andesitic to rhyolitic flows and pyroclastics with interbeds of limestone, volcanic conglomerate and sandstone. They showed 10°-15° counterclockwise rotation of the Arica region, northernmost Chile, with respect to the stable South American platform. These data suggest that the nor- thernmost Chilean region underwent a tectonic rotation at least after the Cretaceous period, as the southern end of the Peruvian block. 1. of the Peruvian block. 1. Introduction The recent paleomagnetic studies of the Central Andean area(PALMER et al., 1980; HEKI, 1983; HEKI et al., 1983, 1984, 1985a, b; KONG et al., 1984)are revealing that the Peruvian Andes has zotated counterclockwise as a nearly rigid "block" giving rise to the present elbow shape of the Andes at the Peru -Chile border(Bolivian orocline; CAREY, 1955). The northernmost part of Chile(the Arica region)is an area of paleomagnetic importance because it accurately cor- responds to the "hinge" of the Bolivian orocline. In this article, we discuss the Cretaceous paleomagnetic data of this region obtained from a red sandstone layer of the Atajana Formation and from a dike swarm(the Arica dike swarm)in- truding into this formation. 2. Introduction The Andean region is a subduction zone characterized by the Peru-Chile trench and the Andean orogenic belt. This subduction zone is a continental arc with no apparent marginal seas at present. Paleomagnetic studies of the Andean belt have been performed to clarify tectonic deformation. In the southernmost part of Andes in Chile the structural trend changes from north-south to northwest-southeast. This change is ascribed to a post Cretaceous deformation by the paleomagnetic method (DALZIEL et a1.,1973; BURNS et al.,1980). In the northernmost part, the trend of the Andean belt changes from northeast-southwest to east-west. MACDONALD and OPDYKE (1972) reported a shift in magnetic declination for the Cretaceous rocks which infers tectonic rotation of northernmost part of the Andean belt. From paleomagnetic and K-Ar geochronological studies PALMER et al. (1980) suggested post-Jurassic counterclockwise rotation of the A

northernmost part of the Andean belt. From paleomagnetic and K-Ar geochronological studies PALMER et al. (1980) suggested post-Jurassic counterclockwise rotation of the Arica region in Central Andes. Further HEKI et al. (1983) carried out intensive sampling and measurement of Cretaceous rocks in Peru and in northernmost Chile. They concluded that the Peruvian block rotated counterclockwise by about 30°after the Cretaceous and that this rotation is a cause of the abrupt change of trend from north-south trend in the Chilean Andes to northwest-southeast of the Peruvian. HEKI et al. (1985) also showed a slight declination shift of Neogene dike swarm in Peru. This deformation is quite interesting on account of its characteristics as an intraplate one, whereas the others in the southernmost and northernmost parts have occurred at edges of the continental 477 478 H. Introduction Secular variation is a significant characteristics of the geomagnetic field. Volcanic rocks are very useful to study paleosecular variation because of their stable thermoremanent magnetization although we obtain spot-reading data. Outcrops of many independent lavas are relatively easy to be found at hotspot areas such as oceanic islands but not in other regions. On the other hand a dike swarm usually occurs in volcanic regions as more than one hundred intrusions of subterranean volcanism. Its activity duration is regarded to be in the order of 105 years similar to that of a stratovolcano (NAKAMURA, 1977). A dike swarm, therefore, probably records paleosecular variation of the geomagnetic field during the time span sufficient to reflect its nature. From this viewpoint we performed a paleomagnetic study on the Ashitaka dike swarm in the southern part of Central Japan and report its result in this paper. 2. Geology of the Ashitaka Volcano and Experimental Procedures The Ashitaka volcano is located southward of Mt. Fuji and westward of Hakone volcano (Fig. 1). According to SAWAMURA (1955), it is constructed with two groups of strata; (1) lower part of older basaltic ejecta and (2) upper one of younger andesitic ejecta. Unfortunately there are no dating results of the Ashitaka volcanic rocks. d southward of Mt. Fuji and westward of Hakone volcano (Fig. 1). According to SAWAMURA (1955), it is constructed with two groups of strata; (1) lower part of older basaltic ejecta and (2) upper one of younger andesitic ejecta. Unfortunately there are no dating results of the Ashitaka volcanic rocks. However these rocks are covered by the Ashitaka loam, which is identified with the Kanto loam supplied by the Fuji and Hakone volcanoes. Volcanism of the Ashitaka is, therefore, considered to have taken place prior to those of the Fuji and Hakone volcanoes, namely several hundreds of thousand years. Stability tests by alternating field and thermal demagnetization reveal the existence of characteristic remanent magnetization, of which directions show significant clockwise deflection; the mean declination shift exceeds 50° in the late Early Miocene members (N6-N8), and is less than 30° in the early Middle Miocene members (N9). This result, compared with the other paleomagnetic data from the Setouchi Miocene Series and the volcanic rocks in the San'in district, suggests that coherent rotation of Southwest Japan began between the late Early Miocene and the early Middle Miocene. Nearly a half of the rotation might have been attained in the stage of Zone N9, which possibly corresponds to the period of the opening and increasing subsidence in the Japan Sea. 1. Introduction Recent paleomagnetic studies (OTOFUJI and MATSUDA, 1983; 1984; HAYASHIDA and ITO, 1984; TORII, 1985) have revealed that

ent paleomagnetic studies (OTOFUJI and MATSUDA, 1983; 1984; HAYASHIDA and ITO, 1984; TORII, 1985) have revealed that Southwest Japan suffered a clockwise rotation at about 15 Ma. The timing of the rotation is much later than previously assumed (KAWAI et al., 1971), and the duration of the rotation seems extremely short. Current research is directed toward increasing the number of paleomagnetic data near the timing of the rotation. This is important for more detailed description of the rotational process, which has a significance in reconstruction of tectonic history around Southwest Japan. Paleomagnetic measurements have been made on samples from the Morozaki Group and the Mizunami Group, typical sequences of the Setouchi Miocene Series sporadically extending in Southwest Japan (Fig. 1). Among them, the late Early Miocene Ichishi Group was shown to have remanent magnetization having easterly deflected declinations (HAYASHIDA and ITO, 1984). The age of the Ichishi Group, about 16 Ma, gives a critical timing for the beginning of the rotation of Southwest Japan. While the Morozaki and Mizunami Groups are correlative to the Ichishi Group in part, the upper members of both groups are suggested to be younger than the Ichishi Group. While the Morozaki and Mizunami Groups are correlative to the Ichishi Group in part, the upper members of both groups are suggested to be younger than the Ichishi Group. The paleomagnetic data from these sections are, therefore, suitable for the purpose mentioned above. section_candidates.excerpt: A and MATSUDA (1985) gave one explanation that the cusp was formed by collisions of the Tanzawa and the Izu Block on the basis of the exotic origin of the Tanzawa Block and the past plate motion. In the Kanto Mountains located on the east wing of the cusp structure, paleomagnetic studies have been scarcely attempted heretofore. The Chichibu Tertiary System, exposed in the central part of the Kanto Mountains, consists of early Miocene marine sediments (Fig. 1). Defining the paleomagnetic direction in this area will give us a better understanding of the relationship between the rotation of Southwest Japan (OTOFUJI et al., 1985) and the formation of the cusp structure. In this paper, we describe the paleomagnetism on the early Miocene marine sediments of the Chichibu Basin and discuss a tectonic process to form the cusp of zonal structure in Central Japan. 2. Geologic Setting The geologic map of the Chichibu Basin is shown in Fig. 2. The Basin extends about 15km in an east-west direction and nearly 12km in a north-south direction, and is filled with early Miocene marine sediments with a thickness of more than 6000 m. The marine sedimentary basin is surrounded on all sides by pre-Tertiary rocks 335 336 H. HYODO and N. NIITsuMA Fig. 1. Index map of the studied area (shaded rect

The pole position corresponding to the mean field direction is close to that observed at the Middle Miocene formations in the peninsula and in the northern part of NE Honshu Island. The dominant orientation of strikes in the Oga dikes represents one of the general trend of the Middle to Late Miocene stress field after the tectonic rotation of NE Honshu Island had completed. 1. Introduction During the last few years paleomagnetic studies have been intensively made on Cenozoic rocks in the Japanese Islands. Tectonic movements of the islands have been discussed based on their results. Major paleomagnetic results of these works were recently reviewed by ToSHA and KoNo (1985) and HIROOKA (1983). Topics on Cenozoic time are summarize

eviewed by ToSHA and KoNo (1985) and HIROOKA (1983). Topics on Cenozoic time are summarized as follows: the directions of the natural remanent magnetizations (NRMs) in pre-Miocene rocks were systematically different from those at present in northeast (NE) and southwest (SW) Honshu Islands. Therefore it is inferred that NE and SW Honshu Islands have undergone counterclockwise and clockwise rotation, respectively (e.g., OTOFUJI and MATSUDA, 1983; OTOFUJI et al., 1985; TOSHA and HAMANO, 1986). The analysis of paleo-stress field is one of the most useful methods to discuss the tectonics, which is derived from the directions of strikes in dike swarms and faults and those of veins in ore deposits. Besides as a stress indicator most of the dikes are composed of igneous rocks and their remanent magnetizations are usually intensive and less disturbable by some late tectonic processes. Hence, dikes are also useful for paleomagnetic works. Introduction The Korean Peninsula is situated between North China platform and trench- island arc-back arc basin systems of Japan and Ryukyu. The former behaves as a stable craton subjected to only epeirogenic movements for over a thousand million years. The latter is one of the most active areas at present on the earth; while new igneous products are added and allochthonous terrains are accreted on the island arc, older geological phenomena have been obscured. In the peculiar situation of the Korean Peninsula, the igneous and sedimentary rocks have been fairly continuously produced from Archaeozoic age to Quaternary, and they have been preserved on the peninsula (UM and REEDMAN, 1975). The Korean Peninsula is, therefore, a rare area where the apparent polar wandering path (APWP) can be expected to be traced back to 2700 Ma. Our ultimate objective is to obtain the paleomagnetic direction change during 2700 Ma from the Korean Peninsula. The aim of the present work is to estimate the paleomagnetic direction for the period between Permian and Cretaceous. †Present address: Earthquake Research Institute, University of Tokyo, Tokyo, Japan. 387 388 Y. Estimation of paleomagnetic direction of the period between Permian and Jurassic is hindered by this. The Cretaceous rocks from the Gyeongsang Supergroup, however, have recorded the paleomagnetic direction at the period of formation of sedimentary rocks during Cretaceous. Some strata in the Hasandong Formation of lower part of the Gyeongsang Supergroup show the reversed magnetization which is presumably ascribed to reversed magnetic polarity epoch of M-series in Mesozoic polarity scale. Paleomagnetic direction of the upper part of the Gyeongsang Supergroup (Middle to Late Cretaceous)is estimated to be Dec=28.4°, Inc=58.2° and α95=6.4°. The pole position of Middle to Late Cretaceous obtained for the Korean Peninsula (202°E, 67°N) is in good agreement with other Cretaceous data for the Asian continent, implying that the Korean Peninsula has not been subjected to rotational movement relative to the Asian continent since Cretaceous. 1. Fourty five examples at 13 sites were collected from Permian strata, 44 samples at 10 sites were from Triassic ones, 91 samples at 23 sites were from Jurassic ones, and 290 samples at 65 sites were from Cretaceous. Two or more specimens 25mm in diameter and 25mm long were prepared from each sample in the laboratory. Natural remanent magnetization (NRM) was measured with a two component SCT cryogenic magnetometer. The stability of remanent magnetization was investi- gated through progressive demagnetization treatment by both thermal and alternat- ing field (AF) methods. Discussion The paleomagnetic directions of the Pre-Cretaceous and Cretaceous periods after bedding correction are compared in Fig. 5. Abrupt change of the paleomagnetic direction is clearly observed between the Jurassic and Cretaceous periods. The westerly direction of the period from Permian to Jurassic changes to easterly one at Cretaceous: The amount of the change is larger than 50°. We interpret that the anomalous westerly direction before Cretaceous is ascribed to the secondary component which was acquired after the rocks had been tilted. The sites were located only in strata with well-defined bedding. In all cases block samples were oriented by a magnetic compass. Fourty five examples at 13 sites were collected from Permian strata, 44 samples at 10 sites were from Triassic ones, 91 samples at 23 sites were from Jurassic ones, and 290 samples at 65 sites were from Cretaceous. Two or more specimens 25mm in diameter and 25mm long were prepared from each sample in the laboratory. Natural remanent magnetization (NRM) was measured with a two component SCT cryogenic magnetometer. The stability of remanent magnetization was investi- gated through progressive demagnetization treatment by both thermal and alternat- ing field (AF) methods. The progressive AF demagnetization was made with a magnetically shielded three axis tumbler and thermal one was with a non-inductively wound electric furnace enclosed in a cylindrical mu-metal shield. One specimen in each site was cleaned as a pilot specimen in a stepwise progression with alternating peak field ranging from 5mT to 50mT. The stability of remanent magnetization was investi- gated through progressive demagnetization treatment by both thermal and alternat- ing field (AF) methods. The progressive AF demagnetization was made with a magnetically shielded three axis tumbler and thermal one was with a non-inductively wound electric furnace enclosed in a cylindrical mu-metal shield. One specimen in each site was cleaned as a pilot specimen in a stepwise progression with alternating peak field ranging from 5mT to 50mT. One or more specimens in each formation was progressively demagnetized with thermal method up to 400℃-600℃. Zijderveld component plots (ZIJDERVELD, 1967) were used to assess the directional stability and coercivity spectrum of each specimen. 4. Introduction The Korean Peninsula is situated between North China platform and trench- island arc-back arc basin systems of Japan and Ryukyu. The former behaves as a stable craton subjected to only epeirogenic movements for over a thousand million years. The latter is one of the most active areas at present on the earth; while new igneous products are added and allochthonous terrains are accreted on the island arc, older geological phenomena have been obscured. In the peculiar situation of the Korean Peninsula, the igneous and sedimentary rocks have been fairly continuously produced from Archaeozoic age to Quaternary, and they have been preserved on the peninsula (UM and REEDMAN, 1975). The Korean Peninsula is, therefore, a rare area where the apparent polar wandering path (APWP) can be expected to be traced back to 2700 Ma. Our ultimate objective is to obtain the paleomagnetic direction change during 2700 Ma from the Korean Peninsula. The aim of the present work is to estimate the paleomagnetic direction for the period between Permian and Cretaceous. †Present address: Earthquake Research Institute, University of Tokyo, Tokyo, Japan. 387 388 Y. (1985) compiled these results, and discussed the process of tectonic rotation of Southwest Japan. This paper describes the paleomagnetic results obtained from Miocene rocks distributed in Fukui Prefecture, the northeastern part (the Hokuriku district) of Southwest Japan, and discusses the tectonic rotation of this area. carrier_investigation_candidates.excerpt: btained from thirty-three (33) sites in metavolcanic rocks and diabase dyke swarms from the ophiolite complex of Thetford Mines in the Appalachians of Southern Quebec (longitude: 7100'-7145'W, latitude: 4545'-4615'N). The metavolcanic rocks are massive or pillowed (mainly) lavas of andesitic and mostly basaltic composition and the dyke swarms are composed of basaltic and doleritic diabases; both lithological groups are metamorphosed to the sub- greenschist (pumpellyite) facies. Pyroclastics, tuffs and volcanic agglomerates are also present in minor quantities. The NRM intensities of the metalavas and diabases are very weak. Mag- netic, titanomagnetite and occasional grains of hematite are the magnetic memory carriers. Native iron was also detected in minute quantities. In order to obtain some pertinent information relative to the stability of the NRM component, stepwise alternating field (AF) demagnetization was con- ducted on 300 of the specimens in the 50-800 Oersteds range and the others were demagnetized at an optimum AF intensity. Approximately 1000 of the specimens underwent thermal treatment in the 100-550C range; thermal de- magnetization was judged less efficient than AF demagnetization and for this reason, the remaining specimens were all AF demagnetized. , Shimane University, Matsue, Japan (Received February 10, 1978) The mean virtual pole position for the Cretaceous granites in South Korea is close to the present geographic pole and is consistent with that for Cretaceous, Pliocene and Pleistocene volcanic rocks from the same region. It also accords with pole positions obtained from Chinese, Siberian and European Cretaceous rocks. From the paleomagnetic data for the granites and volcanic rocks of the Cretaceous, it is concluded that the South Korean land mass has not been subjected to sufficient local tectonic movements to generate a change in the direction of primary magnetic vectors of the granites or of the volcanic rocks since the Cretaceous. This means that although some tectonic movement has taken place in South Korea since the Cretaceous, the movement brought about only vertical block displacements with no sig- nificant tilting or rotational movements. It also suggests that the virtual geomagnetic pole for the Cretaceous rocks in South Korea provides a valid Cretaceous virtual pole position for the Eurasian land mass. 1. Introduction A dike swarm is the subterranean volcanism of more than several tens of intrusions. The subaerial volcanism of a single volcano generally persists its ac- tivity for 104-105 years (e.g., KUNO, 1976). A dike swarm is also considered to be formed in the same time interval as that of the subaerial one (NAKAMURA, 1977). Such time interval is considered to be sufficient to average out the geomagnetic secular variation (HEKI, 1983). Dike rocks are volcanic ones so that they have thermo-remanent magnetization which can yield reliable paleomagnetic data and that we can date them by some radiometric method. Furthermore, we find that dike swarms have occurred at many places throughout geological time. Soper SUMMARY: The well known coastal flexure of central E Greenland, with its associated dyke swarm, affects a thick pile of Tertiary basalts and the underlying basement gneisses. It is a major tectonic/magmatic feature of this 'trailing edge' type continental margin. The original interpretation of Wager & Deer (1938) envisaged the emplacement of the dykes as a fan-shaped swarm in the convex arc of the flexure. Nielsen (1975, 1978) recognized several episodes of dyke emplacement. He interpreted the main swarm (THOL 1) as earlier than the flexure, emplaced vertically into the horizontal basalt pile and subsequently tilted by antithetic faulting during the formation of the flexure. A palaeomagnetic study of the THOL 1 and later dykes shows that the former were emplaced in their present inclined attitude. This discriminates in favour of Wager's interpretation, while remaining consistent with Nielsen's view of the post-flexural magmatic history. Modifications to Nielsen's scheme are suggested to conform with the new evidence, and the implications in relation to the mechanism of flexuring, the timing of tholeiitic magmatism, and the relationship of both to the early spreading history of this sector of the NE Atlantic, are discussed. The coastal flexure in E Greenland is a seaward facing monocline which marks the present coastline for some 600 km between approximately 66 and 70"N (Fig. 1). To the NE of Kangerdlugssuaq, along the Blosseville Kyst, the flexure affects Palaeogene basalts. On the outer headlands for 75 km as far as Jensen Fjord, seaward dips of 35-55" are observed and the mono- cline is associated with an intense swarm of basic dykes which dip landward, roughly normal to the flows. The coastal flexure in E Greenland is a seaward facing monocline which marks the present coastline for some 600 km between approximately 66 and 70"N (Fig. 1). To the NE of Kangerdlugssuaq, along the Blosseville Kyst, the flexure affects Palaeogene basalts. On the outer headlands for 75 km as far as Jensen Fjord, seaward dips of 35-55" are observed and the mono- cline is associated with an intense swarm of basic dykes which dip landward, roughly normal to the flows. section_candidates.excerpt: ll known coastal flexure of central E Greenland, with its associated dyke swarm, affects a thick pile of Tertiary basalts and the underlying basement gneisses. It is a major tectonic/magmatic feature of this 'trailing edge' type continental margin. The original interpretation of Wager & Deer (1938) envisaged the emplacement of the dykes as a fan-shaped swarm in the convex arc of the flexure. Nielsen (1975, 1978) recognized several episodes of dyke emplacement. He interpreted the main swarm (THOL 1) as earlier than the flexure, emplaced vertically into the horizontal basalt pile and subsequently tilted by antithetic faulting during the formation of the flexure. A palaeomagnetic study of the THOL 1 and later dykes shows that the former were emplaced in their present inclined attitude. This discriminates in favour of Wager's interpretation, while remaining consistent with Nielsen's view of the post-flexural magmatic history. Modifications to Nielsen's scheme are suggested to conform with the new evidence, and the implications in relation to the mechanism of flexuring, the timing of tholeiitic magmatism, and the relationship of both to the early spreading history of this sector of the NE Atlantic, are discussed. Duff SUMMARY: Scattered, but stable NRM (natural remanent magnetization) in the Jersey diorite-metagabbro complex, probably acquired during the formation of the complex, can be ascribed to 2 main geological processes: (i) stoping of the late Precambrian or early Cambrian diorites and metagabbros by the Jersey granites, which caused pre-stoping NRM to be dispersed by block rotation and subsidence in the granite melt; this was the largest contributor to palaeomagnetic.matter; (ii) hybridization of the parent gabbro during granite intrusion, which added a dioritic generation of magnetite and its NRM to the NRM carried by the gabbro, and probably also caused variable, partial remagnetization of the gabbroic NRM before stoping. Palaeomagnetic results suggest that the complex NRM of the Jersey diorite-metagabbro complex was not acquired as a VRM (viscous remanent magnetization) in a recent geomagnetic field. Rather, the explanation of the unusual scatter of stable NRM directions in these rocks is probably to be sought in the well- documented sequence of geological events that gov- erned the formation of the diorite-metagabbro com- plex (Wells & Wooldridge 1931; Bishop 1954; Wells & Bishop 1955; Key 1974). This compl

Origin of the within-block scatter Microprobe and optical results (Duff 1978) strongly suggest that the within-block scatter of NRM direc- tions and related variable demagnetization trends (Figs 2 & 3) reflect the highly variable overprinting of an original gabbroic NRM during hybridization of the gabbro (dioritization) by the Jersey granites. The re- sulting multicomponent NRM may have originated in either or both of the following ways: (i) variable partial remagnetization of primary gabbroic NRM; (ii) acquisition by magnetites grown during dioritization of a dioritic NRM in addition to that already present in the primary gabbroic titanomagnetites. Typically, the original gabbroic assemblage has been altered to a dioritic assemblage at temperatures of the upper amphibolite or granulite facies (Key 1974). At these temperatures (>500" C) only a small amount of the original remanence may survive in grains with high blocking temperatures (Pullaiah et al. 1975), so it is likely that the original gabbro was entirely or partially remagnetized during hybridization by the granite melt. Badham SUMMARY: The Lizard Complex of SW England has recently been interpreted as representing a fragment of oceanic lithosphere that was thrust on to the continental crust of S Cornwall in the Devonian as a result of tectonic processes at a convergent plate margin. A palaeomagnetic study has been carried out on the ultramafics. gabbros and dykes of the E coast section to examine possible tectonic movements that might have been associated with this history of formation. A component of stable magnetization having a shallow to intermediate negative inclination and a SSW declination has been identified in each of these lithologies. This direction is similar to the Permian geomagnetic field direction for SW England, and one interpretation of the results is that the Lizard rocks were remagnetized in the early Permian, perhaps as a result of heating associated with emplacement of the Variscan batholiths. However. no mineralogical or other evidence for widespread heating of the Lizard Complex in the Permian has yet been identified. A component of stable magnetization having a shallow to intermediate negative inclination and a SSW declination has been identified in each of these lithologies. This direction is similar to the Permian geomagnetic field direction for SW England, and one interpretation of the results is that the Lizard rocks were remagnetized in the early Permian, perhaps as a result of heating associated with emplacement of the Variscan batholiths. However. no mineralogical or other evidence for widespread heating of the Lizard Complex in the Permian has yet been identified. This magnetozone has a thickness of some 15 m and its upper boundary is well defined in the Yaverland section but is obscured in the Shepherd's Chine Section due to cliff slumping. The lower boundary is well established in both sections and lies some 15 m above the Barnes High Sandstone Member in the Shepherd's Chine section and 12m above this unit at Yaverland. This boundary provides a useful chron-stratigraphic datum. A comparison with established geomagnetic polarity timescales for the Cretaceous indicates that the Vectis magnetozone may be correlated either with Lower Aptian reverse polarity Chron CM-0 or with Lower Barremian Chron CM-l, with the former being the more likely. ORS) is the largest of the Devonian massifs in Norway (Fig. l), and comprises c. 25 km of mainly axially-deposited alluvial grey sandstones and siltstones interfingering with marginal fan- conglomerates (Steel et al. 1985). Plant and fish fossils found in the upper part of the succession indicate an upper Lower Devonian age. The great apparent stratigraphical thickness, alluvial sedimentation and basin asymmetry, together with repetitions of basin-wide, upward-coarsening sequences associated with lateral extension, were among the factors that led Bryhni (1964, 1978) and Steel and co-workers (see review in Steel et al. 1985) to the conclusion that the Hornelen ‘Basin’ was tectonically generated. The basin developed with a principal component of hinge-faulting or dextral oblique shear along, or close to, the present northern marginal fault (Figs lb & 2). Depocentres were considered to have migrated eastwards with time, in an opposite direction to the palaeoflow indicators. Over much of the outcrop of the Devonian sediments there are few penetrative effects of deformation. The rocks abound in sedimentary structures, and primary features, such as bedding, dominate the outcrop pattern. In this novel extensional model, collapse of the footwall, i.e. the Mal~y Fault (Hossack 1984) or Nordfjord-Sogn detachment (Norton 1986), is considered to have led to sedimentary deposition in the hanging wall. Eastward onlap relationships originated as a roll-over anticline which accompanied the listric faulting. ORS) is the largest of the Devonian massifs in Norway (Fig. l), and comprises c. 25 km of mainly axially-deposited alluvial grey sandstones and siltstones interfingering with marginal fan- conglomerates (Steel et al. 1985). Plant and fish fossils found in the upper part of the succession indicate an upper Lower Devonian age. The great apparent stratigraphical thickness, alluvial sedimentation and basin asymmetry, together with repetitions of basin-wide, upward-coarsening sequences associated with lateral extension, were among the factors that led Bryhni (1964, 1978) and Steel and co-workers (see review in Steel et al. 1985) to the conclusion that the Hornelen ‘Basin’ was tectonically generated. The basin developed with a principal component of hinge-faulting or dextral oblique shear along, or close to, the present northern marginal fault (Figs lb & 2). Depocentres were considered to have migrated eastwards with time, in an opposite direction to the palaeoflow indicators. Over much of the outcrop of the Devonian sediments there are few penetrative effects of deformation. The rocks abound in sedimentary structures, and primary features, such as bedding, dominate the outcrop pattern. Detailed sampling within the Late Permian- Middle Triassic Narrabeen Group has been carried out north and south of Sydney at coastal outcrops between Wybung Head and Coal Cliff (Fig. 1). The beds are essentially flat lying, regional dips of 1 to 2 probably being the result of Tertiary warping. The lower units of the Narrabeen Group in the coastal section north of Sydney are characterised by conglomerates and coarse grey, green, and buff coloured sandstones. The sediments were carried by streams and deposited in channels located between flood plain fine sands and thin bands of red claystone formed in part by overbank deposition. Higher in the section a relatively persistent red claystone horizon is encountered; in the northern coastal section this is known as the Patonga Claystone and a similar horizon (though possibly younger) south of Sydney is the Bald Hill Claystone (HERBERT, 1970). 2. The beds are essentially flat lying, regional dips of 1 to 2 probably being the result of Tertiary warping. Geology and Sampling A 25-km coastal strip of largely volcanic rocks west of Tramore, County Waterford, forms part of a wider belt of Cambrian to Silurian volcanism in south-eastern Ireland which peaked in the Upper Ordovician. The rocks are largely submarine and are considered (PHILLIPS et a1.,1976; STILLMAN, 1978; STILLMAN and WILLIAMS, 1978) to have been erupted at a continental plate margin related to a SE-dipping subduction zone and developing arc-trench system that formed part of a Lower Paleozoic Proto-Atlantic ocean; such a subduction system was postulated earlier for the Lake District and Wales (FITTON and HUGHES, 1970).
